h1: Amps to kW Calculator (and kW to Amps)
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: amps
fields.label: Current
fields.hint: Measured or rated current. For three-phase, the current in one line wire.

fields.name: mode
fields.label: Supply type
fields.hint: Most homes are single-phase; shops, tubewells and large houses are often three-phase.

fields.name: volts
fields.label: Voltage
fields.hint: Leave blank for 230 V single-phase or 400 V three-phase line to line. For DC enter the battery or system voltage.

fields.name: pf
fields.label: Power factor
fields.hint: About 0.8 for motors and mixed loads, 1 for heaters. Ignored for DC.

answer: {{in.amps|int}} amps on a {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase supply is {{out.kw|2}} kW at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}. kW = amps × volts × power factor ÷ 1,000, with √3 added for three-phase, where {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A per line at {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V is {{ex.2.out.kw|2}} kW. For kW to amps, reverse it: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor).
how: {{in.amps|int}} A × {{out.volts|int}} V × {{out.pf|2}} ÷ 1,000 = {{out.kw|2}} kW of real power. The apparent power is {{out.va|int}} VA, the load the cable, breaker and any generator or UPS must carry. On three-phase the result is multiplied by √3; on DC the power factor is one.
key_facts: kW = amps × volts × power factor ÷ 1,000 (single-phase). {{in.amps|int}} A at {{in.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{out.pf|2}} is {{out.kw|2}} kW.

On a three-phase {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V supply, {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A per line at a power factor of {{ex.2.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.2.out.kw|2}} kW, about three times the single-phase figure for the same amps.
A {{ex.1.in.amps|int}} A single-phase supply at {{ex.1.out.volts|int}} V carries {{ex.1.out.kw|2}} kW at a power factor of {{ex.1.in.pf|2}}.
kW is real power, kVA is apparent power and amps is current: kW = kVA × power factor, and amps follow from kVA and the voltage.

formula.text: Amps to kW: kW = V × I × PF ÷ 1,000 (×√3 for three-phase).  kW to amps: I = kW × 1,000 ÷ (V × PF) (÷√3 for three-phase)
lines: I = current in amps (per line for three-phase)
V = voltage: phase-to-neutral for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase, battery voltage for DC
PF = power factor (1 for DC and heaters)

sections.h2: Amps to kW on single-phase and three-phase
p: Multiply the amps by the volts and the power factor, then divide by 1,000. {{in.amps|int}} A on {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase is {{out.kw|2}} kW. On three-phase the same current in each line carries √3 times more power at the higher line voltage: {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A per line at {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V is {{ex.2.out.kw|2}} kW.

Reverse the same formula: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor) on single-phase, and amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (√3 × volts × power factor) on three-phase. In the table below, find the kW nearest your load and read the current on the same row. For an exact figure, the watts to amps calculator does single-phase and DC, and the 3 phase amps calculator takes kW or kVA directly.

sections.h2: {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} amps to kW and {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} amp to kW
p: A {{ex.0.in.amps|int}} A single-phase circuit at {{ex.0.out.volts|int}} V carries {{ex.0.out.kw|2}} kW at a power factor of {{ex.0.in.pf|2}}. A {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} A three-phase main breaker at {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} V passes up to {{ex.3.out.kw|2}} kW at a power factor of {{ex.3.in.pf|2}}. These are ceilings for the breaker, not loads to run continuously.

kW is the real power that does work and that the meter bills. kVA is the apparent power, volts × amps ÷ 1,000, which cables, transformers, generators and UPS units must carry. Amps is the current itself. For a heater kW and kVA are equal; for motors and mixed loads kW = kVA × power factor, so the same kW needs more amps when the power factor is low.

mistakes: Forgetting the power factor. Volts × amps gives kVA; kW is lower for motors, ACs and mixed loads (about {{d.pf_mixed|2}} of the kVA).
Using the single-phase formula on three-phase. Three-phase needs √3 and the line-to-line voltage ({{d.v_3ph|int}} V), with the current of one line.
Dividing by 1,000 twice or not at all. Watts ÷ 1,000 = kW; check the answer is the size you expect.
Treating a breaker's kW as the load you can run all day. Long-running loads need a margin below the breaker rating.
safety: These conversions are for planning. A licensed electrician should confirm the cable, breaker and meter connection before any load is added to a supply.

faq.a: {{out.kw|2}} kW on {{in.volts|int}} V single-phase at a power factor of {{out.pf|2}}, or {{ex.0.out.kw|2}} kW for a heating load. On three-phase {{d.v_3ph|int}} V, {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} A per line is {{ex.3.out.kw|2}} kW at the same power factor.

faq.q: What is the kW to amps formula?
faq.a: Single-phase: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor). Three-phase: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (√3 × line-to-line volts × power factor). DC: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ volts.

faq.q: How many amps is one kW?
faq.a: It depends on the voltage and power factor: amps = kW × 1,000 ÷ (volts × power factor). On {{d.v_1ph|int}} V single-phase that is a few amps per kW, on {{d.v_3ph|int}} V three-phase fewer per line, and on a battery many more. The table above gives exact pairs.

faq.q: How many kW is {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} amps on three-phase?
faq.a: {{ex.3.out.kw|2}} kW at {{ex.3.out.volts|int}} V and a power factor of {{ex.3.in.pf|2}}. On single-phase {{d.v_1ph|int}} V, {{ex.3.in.amps|int}} A is much less; the table shows both.

faq.q: How do I convert amps to kW on three-phase?
faq.a: Multiply √3 × line-to-line volts × amps per line × power factor, then divide by 1,000. {{ex.2.in.amps|int}} A at {{ex.2.out.volts|int}} V and {{ex.2.in.pf|2}} is {{ex.2.out.kw|2}} kW.

faq.q: What is the difference between kW, kVA and amps?
faq.a: kW is real power, kVA is apparent power and amps is current. kW = kVA × power factor; kVA = volts × amps ÷ 1,000 on single-phase (× √3 on three-phase).
